40962-prophecies-of-robert-nixon-mother-:
This chapbook gathers the Prophecies of Robert Nixon, Mother Shipton, and Martha the Gipsy, published in London for the booksellers. Nixon, called the Cheshire prophet, comes first. His life fills the opening pages. Then come his original predictions, others copied from old pamphlets, and his Cheshire prophecy at large, with remarks on how it has been fulfilled.

Mother Shipton's life and prophecies take the largest share of the book. Martha's prophecies and a remarkable fulfilment close it. Between the prophets stand extracts on the French Revolution and sermons by Gill, with an extraordinary prediction related by Wesley. Such collections sold for pennies at fairs and doors for two centuries. They kept village prophets in print long after their deaths, and readers tested every new war or king against the old verses.
54716-the-horse-in-america-a-practical-t:
John Gilmer Speed wrote this treatise, The Horse in America, printed at New York in 1905. Its subtitle promises a practical account of the various types common in the United States, with something of their history and varying traits. A front picture shows the trotting mare Flora Temple, called queen of the trotting turf for more than six years, the first trotter to beat the two-twenty mile. Speed dedicates the book to a friend whose inherited love of horses was strengthened by study and practice.

Chapter one looks far back, to prehistoric and early horses. Fossils show, Speed writes, that horse-kind swarmed over America in an early age, yet none remained when Columbus came. The first fossils baffled the naturalists: a beast under two feet tall, with a spreading five-toed foot fitted for marshy ground.
68224-synthetic-resins-and-their-raw-mat: Report number 131 of the United States Tariff Commission bears the title Synthetic Resins and Their Raw Materials. The hosted pages open with the Commission's list of recent reports, priced in cents, on goods from dressed furs and zippers to tuna fish and wood pulp. Such reports went to the President or the Senate under the Tariff Act of 1930. This one surveys the young synthetic resin trade and its raw materials, for the men who set the duties.
britannica-1911-cuyp:
Cuyp, the name of a Dutch family of painters at Dordrecht, is covered in an art entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The family produced two generations of painters. Jacob Gerritsz Cuyp, born about 1575, was the first to win fame. He was taught by Abraham Bloemaert of Utrecht.

Jacobs pictures are little known, but his portraits are praised as honest and true. He painted busts, groups in rooms, and scenes in gardens. In works with children he liked to add toys and pets, such as a lamb or a goat. His son Albert Cuyp, born in 1620, became the famed name of the house. Albert wed a rich widow in 1658 and held a seat linked to his lands. In 1672 he was placed on a list from which the stadtholder chose the rulers of Dordrecht.
